title: Jump first (Sotah 37a)
hook: the tribes hesitate at the sea; Nachshon jumps in first
tomorrow: Joseph's coffin is lost somewhere in Egypt. who still knows where?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses' last moment: his soul hesitated, and God came close and took it with a kiss. Taken with a kiss. Today, a hesitation of a different kind, at the edge of the sea.

A wedding, the music's on, and the dance floor is empty. Everyone is at the edges, holding a drink, waiting. Nobody wants to be first. Then one person walks out alone, a little awkward, and within a song the floor is full. The Talmud tells that moment at the edge of the Red Sea, with a lot more water.
screen: `AN EMPTY DANCE FLOOR.` → `NOBODY WANTS TO BE FIRST.` → `ONE PERSON WALKS OUT.`

segments.voice: Egypt's army behind them, water in front. Rabbi Yehuda says each tribe stood at the edge saying: not me first. Then Nachshon, son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah, jumped in, and the water rose to his neck. Meanwhile Moses was praying at length, and God answered him with Exodus: "Wherefore criest thou unto Me? speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward." Right beside that, Rabbi Meir tells it the other way: the tribes raced to be first, and Benjamin got there. The Talmud keeps both. Nachshon's is the version people repeat. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in this telling, the sea doesn't split so people can step in. Someone steps in, and then it splits. Now this week's neighbor. Christians tell a story with the same wet feet. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus comes walking on the water toward his disciples' boat and says, Come. "And when Peter was come down out of the ship, he walked on the water, to go to Jesus." What's shared is the step itself: leaving the safe place before the water makes sense. And an honest difference. Peter steps out because Jesus calls him, and when he begins to sink, Jesus catches him; Christians read it as a story of trusting Jesus. Nachshon goes uncalled, while Moses is still praying, and the Talmud reads his jump as the moment a whole people starts to move. Two stories, one shared courage: going first.
screen: `NOT ME FIRST.` · `NACHSHON JUMPS. THEN IT SPLITS.` · `PETER: COME DOWN OUT OF THE SHIP.` · `SHARED STEP, DIFFERENT CALL.` · then, large: `JUMP FIRST.`

segments.voice: Stand up, if you can, feet together, as if at the edge of the water. Name one thing you've been waiting for someone else to start: an apology, a plan, a hard conversation. Take one step forward, and with it decide the first small move you'll make. Stay standing there, on the far side of the step, while the sit runs.
screen: `STAND AT THE EDGE.` · `NAME WHAT YOU'RE WAITING ON.` · `ONE STEP FORWARD.`

segments.voice: Jump first: Nachshon at the sea, in the water to his neck before it split, so the others could follow.
Your line: jump first. Others start moving once someone does. Thirty-five down, five to go.

howItsDone: In Jewish speech a 'Nachshon' is someone who goes first, and the crossing of the sea is read aloud in synagogue during Passover and in the weekly Torah cycle. Christians read Peter's walk on the water in Matthew 14.

chat.meaning: Both stories honor leaving the safe place first. Peter steps out at Jesus' call and is caught; Nachshon jumps before the sea splits, so a people can move.

Nachshon.meaning: a leader of Judah who, in the Talmud, jumps in first

Amminadab.meaning: Nachshon's father, of the tribe of Judah

Rabbi Meir.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah era

Peter.meaning: a disciple of Jesus, a fisherman, in the Gospels

Unity thread (wisdom day): shared, the step into the water before it makes sense; honest difference, Peter is called by Jesus and caught, Nachshon goes uncalled and his jump moves a people. Neither is ranked; not 'the same story'.
